title: Traveling Route 66 in the Age of Data Centers
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
In its heyday, Route 66 was a road of opportunities and dreams. Today, it’s a highway of ghosts, a symbol of what once was, although it still attracts visitors. For Current Affairs, Jesse Wright reflects on America’s historic highway in a time of artificial intelligence, when so much land across the country is being bought up, repurposed, and turned into data centers. Wright, who traveled the road from Chicago to Santa Monica, asks: What will these massive centers leave behind?

But what is new, perhaps, is the utter absence of even having been at all. The data centers’ legacy will be nothing. Their absence will be complete. Computer hallucinations leave no room for the dreams of humans. In 100 years, there will be nothing. Nobody will want to spend their vacation touring endless rooms full of rusty server racks.

More stories about road trips

The Real Life Mermaids of Florida’s Weeki Wachee Springs

Jack Burke | Huck | July 2, 2026 | 2,317 words

“The fragility and fantasy of old America.”

Grant Achatz and Sam Lim Achatz; Ryan RedCorn; and Dave Holmes

“The country’s legendary main street celebrates its centennial against the backdrop of the nation’s 250th birthday. Could there be a better time for a road trip?”

Are We There Yet?

James Wade | Texas Highways | May 1, 2026 | 3,479 words

“A family trips and stumbles across 3,000 miles of Texas.”

Will Dad and I Ever See Texas the Same Way?

title: A Rare Chance to See a Turner Masterpiece Up Very Close
author: @NewYorker
content:
Racking up the air miles, requiring no sleep, and still in tremendous shape, a distinguished visitor—a real piece of work—is arriving in New York and staying on Madison Avenue. Callers will be received from Saturday, November 7th, through Wednesday the 18th. High rollers are especially welcome, but anyone can come.

“Rome, from Mount Aventine” is an oil painting by Turner—or, to give him his full due, Joseph Mallord William Turner, R.A. It measures just over three feet by four; owners of a fifty-five-inch TV will have a rough idea of the size, although the colors in the Turner would make the engineers at Samsung break down and cry. Should you wish to install the work in your home, the happy news is that it needs no internet connection; the only slight drawback is that it may cost you north of sixty-seven million dollars. That is the conservative estimate placed on the painting by Sotheby’s, in whose New York branch it will temporarily hang, before going under the gavel at the company’s London auction house, on December 9th. Somebody, somewhere, is going to have a poorer but happier Christmas.

Nowadays, it is not uncommon for single paintings awaiting sale to go on tour like rock stars. “Salvator Mundi”—a portrait of Jesus, which, depending on your taste and your scholarly instinct, was wholly or partly or minimally painted by Leonardo da Vinci—travelled to Hong Kong, London, San Francisco, and Singapore before being hawked at Christie’s in New York, in 2017. It sold for more than four hundred and fifty million dollars and then went quiet; reportedly, it now resides in Saudi Arabia, although, for all we know, it could be hanging out at the Chateau Marmont and running up a bar tab for the ages. Similarly, “Rome, from Mount Aventine” has been on the road. Before New York, it was in Hong Kong; before Hong Kong, in London; and, before London, in Rome, where it was displayed in lonely splendor at the Palazzo Rondinini, between the River Tiber and the Villa Borghese gardens. The painting was, so to speak, returning to its place of birth.

The date of that birth is not easy to pin down. The first stirrings of “Rome, from Mount Aventine” can be traced to a trip that Turner made to Italy in 1828, the third of seven visits to the country. At the age of fifty-three, he arrived in Rome in October, having set off from England in August. (Imprudently, he delayed his return until January, 1829. When his stagecoach foundered in the alpine snows, Turner calmly rendered the scene in a dramatic watercolor; what was a disaster for his fellow-travellers was, for him, an aesthetic opportunity.) During his months in the city, he made several intricate sketches that would contribute to “Rome, from Mount Aventine.” By good fortune, they still exist, in the possession of London’s Tate Gallery, and can be compared with the finished painting. But how long was it in the finishing?

If you want to see a field of battle being keenly contested, try the dating of paintings by art historians. Quarrels over dates are not as lethally implacable as quarrels over attribution—who painted what?—but, then, nothing is. The fact that the wood of the frame over which “Rome, from Mount Aventine” is stretched, for instance, appears to be of Italian manufacture could mean that Turner began mapping out the work in Rome. If so, he must have had it in mind, and perhaps in hand, by the time he left the place, and then gone back to the canvas in the years to come, though the pattern of his labors is unclear. Turner was hardly alone among artists in devoting the same intensity of care to the enrichment of a painting that others give to the rearing of a child.

What we do know is that the painting was finally exhibited at the Royal Academy, in London, in 1836, and that it was bought by Hugh Munro, one of Turner’s most important patrons, who had originally commissioned it. Munro was a fascinating specimen: a wealthy Scot, though not a nobleman, he didn’t lord it over Turner so much as befriend him, despite being more than twenty years his junior, and the two of them even journeyed through France and Italy together, drawing and painting as they went, with the artist acting as his patron’s informal tutor. A shy soul, Munro had inherited his fortune via an uncle only after the untimely death of the latter’s sons. One was killed by a tiger and the other by a shark.

So, what did Munro get for his money, when he bought “Rome, from Mount Aventine”? An amalgam of the precise and the visionary, such as Turner alone could concoct. We find ourselves on the southernmost of the city’s seven hills, the Aventine, gazing at once downward, across, and afar. Immediately below us, a bald-headed friar passes; a young woman greets him on her knees, raising her hands in supplication. Miles away, in the distance, on the left, another dome—that of St. Peter’s—breaks the horizon and rhymes with the friar’s pate. In between is the slow, broad blue-violet curve of the Tiber, whose waters seem to rise like vapors and cling to the buildings on the shore: a capillary action, and an ideal match for the way in which the Roman past, refusing to evaporate, insists on climbing and sticking to the stones, and the human lives, of the present day.

The painting is commanded by an umbrella pine, which arches high into the butter-yellow heavens, on the right, leaning over the heart of the composition. Framing by tree is a well-worn trick, perfected by Claude Lorrain, whom Turner revered, and deployed by Turner long before he ever went to Rome (as in his depiction of Aeneas and the Cumaean Sibyl, from 1814-15, now housed in the Yale Center for British Art). The slanting trunk of the pine, in “Rome, from Mount Aventine,” is answered, at a near-right angle, on the left, by a not quite horizontal block of white, set back from the river. This is the Ospizio di San Michele a Ripa, in Trastevere. Approach the painting, close enough to see the scratchy hatchings with which Turner enlivens the walls and roofs of the riverside dwellings, and you will notice three tiny awnings, left open, on the Ospizio’s long façade: grace notes to interrupt any threat of monotone. Our eyes deserve to be occupied.

All this was too much for some early viewers. The painting was disdained, by a critic in Blackwood’s magazine, as “a most unpleasant mixture, wherein white gambouge and raw sienna are, with childish execution, daubed together.” Gambouge, or gamboge, is a toxic yellow-gold pigment derived from resin. In other words, the quality that now pulls us most startlingly into “Rome, from Mount Aventine”—its all-pervading luminescence—is exactly what unnerved the reviewer, who claimed that Turner “has robbed the sun of its birthright to cast shadows.” As so often, hostility is more suggestive than acclaim; despite the darkness in the southeast quarter of the painting, it is overbearingly bright, as if the Eternal City were itself a source of light. In a postscript to the controversy, the young John Ruskin was so incensed by the article in Blackwood’s that he leaped to the defense of Turner, who forwarded his broadside to Munro. It was the opening salvo in what would become Ruskin’s lifelong campaign to appraise, and to praise, Turner’s art. If you buy this painting, therefore, you are getting not just a glorious staging post in Turner’s career, plus a chapter in the long saga of Italy worship, but, also, for what it’s worth, a footnote in the history of criticism.

In mid-October, in London, I spent an hour with “Rome, from Mount Aventine.” To see it in the flesh is to realize how much blood is lost in even the most exacting of reproductions. The scumbled clouds at the top left, barely perceptible on the page of a book, could be read as more Venetian than Roman—rose-pink against blue, as in the dawn sky of a Giovanni Bellini. The texture there is notably thick; according to Julian Gascoigne, a specialist in British art at Sotheby’s, “a lot of that is knife work,” meaning that the paint was applied with a palette knife. It looks as fresh as cream. Gascoigne and I stood in front of the picture, the condition of which, barring a few cracks, is almost laughably untouched by time. No ill-advised Victorian restorations, no heavy varnishings, no smuts from candle smoke. Also, it’s unlined; that is to say, no extra backing was glued to the rear of the canvas to lend it support. (Such a process, as Gascoigne told me, “can seriously diminish the surface.”) The glow of many Turners has dwindled, thanks to unstable pigments, but here is an immaculate exception. Were its creator to see it now, he would presumably feel gratified. Indeed, as an inveterate meddler, he would probably pick up his brushes and carry on the good work.

The bidding for “Rome, from Mount Aventine,” in December, is unlikely to be as serene as the atmosphere that reigns within the frame. Having tempted prospective buyers during its global stops, the picture will have cranked up the force of their coveting. It is quite possible that, once sold, like “Salvator Mundi,” it will vanish from sight; I like to think that, in a nod to the family of its first owner, it might wind up on the walls of a Bond villain’s hideout, to complement his handsome gathering of tigers and sharks. (Keep in mind that a treasure that goes into a private collection can always come back out.) On the whole, though, it would be more fitting if, like a pilgrim, the painting found its way to Rome. “This is Turner’s love letter to the Rome that inspired the Grand Tour,” Gascoigne said to me. “More than just giving you a visual representation of the topography of the city, he’s trying to evoke the sensation of actually being there.”

As for the competition, it would be surprising if the Getty Museum, in Los Angeles, were not to enter the fray. “Rome, from Mount Aventine” would make a natural companion for “Modern Rome – Campo Vaccino,” another of Turner’s dreamlike cityscapes, from the same era, which the museum already owns. Reuniting the pair would be like getting Romulus back together with Remus. Both pictures were bought from Munro’s estate, in 1878, by Lord Rosebery, who could afford them, having recently taken the wise precaution of marrying a Rothschild; the couple went so far as to pause their honeymoon, in Scotland, to view the paintings. (As the new bride explained, in a letter, “Archie wanted to see the Turners.”) Rosebery was later to become the British Prime Minister, though for little more than a year. Painting being a more enduring art than politics, both “Modern Rome – Campo Vaccino” and “Rome, from Mount Aventine” stayed in his family for generations, until this century. The first went to the Getty, in 2010, and the second, in 2014, to buyers unnamed, for around forty million dollars.

But why fight for this Turner, the galleries and the billionaires will ask, rather than any other? Because, as Gascoigne said, “It is now one of the last great handful of masterpieces, particularly from the late period of his work, that remain in private hands.” Soon it will pass to other hands; for the moment, though not for long, it is out in the open. Go and see it on Madison Avenue, and, for good measure, observe how other people see it, too. In “Modern Painters,” Ruskin wrote, “I am fond of standing by a bright Turner in the Academy, to listen to the unintentional compliments of the crowd—‘What a glaring thing!’ ‘I declare I can’t look at it!’ ‘Don’t it hurt your eyes?’—expressed as if they were in the constant habit of looking the sun full in the face.” We all need dazzling these days. Catch the light while you can. ♦

title: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s Linguistic Art
author: @NewYorker
content:
Also: Bill Irwin and Rachel Bloom in Molière, a new movie from Kogonada, the torrid post-punk of Sweeping Promises, and more.

November 6, 2026

It’s taken me some days to write about Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s show at Artists Space, because I didn’t want to face the fact that she’s no longer around to keep growing as an artist, a thinker, and a woman. Cha explored her deep interest in language among distinct cultures—including that of her native South Korea, where she grew up, and of the United States, where she moved, in 1962, when she was eleven—with video, performance, and multimedia installations. “Theresa Hak Kyung Cha: Multiple Offerings” (organized by the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, and on through Nov. 21) is the first retrospective of Cha’s work in twenty-five years, and I can’t imagine a more beautiful curatorial vision. Everything about it—placement, context, sound, moving image—works to create a kind of holistic portrait of an artist who was as devoted to image as she was to language, and to show the ways in which each amplifies the other.

Indeed, her mysterious and uncategorizable book “Dictee,” from 1982, features a number of women talking, ranging from Joan of Arc to the artist’s mother, who lived through Japanese rule, when Korean could not be spoken in public. In “Dictee,” and in her performances, many of which are featured in “Multiple Offerings,” Cha’s and other women’s voices rise out of bodies that have lived through some form of oppression to come out on the other side as whole and true. One walks away from this historic show deeply moved by its singularity, and angry: in 1982, shortly before her first exhibition at Artists Space was scheduled to open, Cha, who was working on a series of photographs about her time employed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, was murdered.—Hilton Als

Dance

The first part of “Adaku”—a dance-theatre trilogy by Okwui Okpokwasili and Peter Born that spools out a speculative vision rooted in a pre-colonial African village—ended with wailing, as a beloved daughter was caught up in the transatlantic slave trade. Part 2, “She Shivers with It,” which has its New York début at BAM, starts with that choral cry and fast-forwards into an alternate present, tapping into embodied memory to trace the lineage of the lost daughter. Amid two hundred feet of snaking red coil, the ritualistic performance lingers in pain but also mines the humor in a magical hairdresser.—Brian Seibert (BAM Fisher; Nov. 11-15.)

Dance

Paul Taylor Dance Company has lately diversified its repertory considerably. This season includes new and recent pieces by the resident artists Robert Battle and Lauren Lovette; an example of mid-century psychedelia by Alwin Nikolais; and “Messengers, Maidens and the End of Something Else,” by the jokey postmodernist Pam Tanowitz. A tongue-in-cheek exploration of the classical-music repertoire, the dance pairs the first and fourth movements of Schubert’s “Death and the Maiden” quartet with a bright palette of movement and color. Those who come for Taylor will be rewarded with rare revivals of “Arabesque,” from 1999, which is set to a Debussy composition that suggests prettiness but soon reveals something darker, and “Byzantium,” from 1984, which probes the degenerate sides of society.—Marina Harss (David H. Koch Theatre; through Nov. 22.)

Broadway

Molière collapsed onstage while performing the lead role of his last play, “The Imaginary Invalid,” and died hours later. That it’s a sendup of doctors and medicine is an irony worthy of its author. Brandon J. Dirden’s revival, for Roundabout, features Bill Irwin (who also adapted the text from Doug Skinner’s translation) as the lead: a perfectly healthy hypochondriac exploited by greedy, bullshitting physicians. Irwin’s performance is a marvel of physical and vocal comedy, complemented by Crystal A. Dickinson as his sweet-talking, gold-digging wife; Rachel Bloom as the sly servant who sees and fixes all; and a bloviating Brooks Ashmanskas, double-cast as two of the quacks. In its whirligig puncturing of pretense, this sumptuous production not only honors Molière’s spirit but makes it felt, offering us ninety minutes with him in comedy heaven.—Dan Stahl (Haimes; through Nov. 22.)

Off Broadway

In the new musical “Midnight,” Rail (Todrick Hall, who also wrote and directed), an enslaved Black man, falls in love with Richard (Jeremy Beloate), a white man he works for; in the second act, they swap social placements, so that Rail is the wealthy landowner and Richard the enslaved worker. (They remain in love.) Even if the songs go on twice as long as is necessary to the plot, the singing is a considerable pleasure, with Kennedy Caughell bringing a spirited assurance to her turn as Scarlet, an imperious Southern belle, while Charlotte Odusanya imbues Lily Rose—a young woman wooed by Rail’s “pretty eyes”—with a lambent sweetness. Hall’s ambitious show is concerned with racial legibility and manipulation, but he’s threading with a dull needle.—Rhoda Feng (Daryl Roth; through Jan. 3.)

Movies

Reappropriating the means of production after two elaborate movies, the director Kogonada filmed “Zi” in Hong Kong, shooting on the fly with a main cast of three and a scant crew to match. The results are as daring as the method; the title character, a Hong Kong-born violinist (Michelle Mao), is awaiting test results about a possible brain tumor. In a variation on Agnès Varda’s “Cléo from 5 to 7,” Zi has hallucinations—seeing flashes of her future self, as though mentally stuck in her own past—but a chance connection with an American wanderer (Haley Lu Richardson) and a Korean scientist (Jin Ha) offers hope: the trio’s lurching, passionate overnight ramble helps diagnose a metaphysical malady. The filmmaker’s ardently curious vision of the cityscape links inner lives to history, self-images to aesthetics.—Richard Brody (Metrograph through Nov. 15, and in limited release.)

Post-Punk

Since its inception, in 2019, the torrid band Sweeping Promises has been a project about the act of creating. Its partners, Lira Mondal and Caufield Schnug, started up on a whim when a jam sesh in an abandoned science lab conjured their first song, which became the title track for their 2020 début, “Hunger for a Way Out.” The band was imagined as a space beyond the duo’s other musical projects to “capture the exhilaration of writing songs in the moment,” as Mondal put it, and the music is governed primarily by impulses—it’s lo-fi and punk, possessing a free spirit and a resourceful nature. Their most recent album, “You Say I Romanticize,” reaffirms their core drive with songs more explicitly about committing to an artistic life.—Sheldon Pearce (Baby’s All Right; Nov. 11.)

Taran Dugal excavates cocktails in Bushwick.

Brooklyn night life is full of imposing figures: brutish bouncers, cool-kid carousers, the rare haughty bartender. But it wasn’t until this summer’s opening of the Museum, a low-lit cocktail lounge in Bushwick, that barflies had to contend with a T. rex—or, at least, a replica of one, whose skull is mounted on a table in the back room. On a recent weekend, three friends sat to the dino’s right, trying their best to ignore his unmistakable glower. They’d begun their evening in the Gift Shop, a cozy parlor up front serving drinks and finger foods, before making their way through the establishment’s Exhibition Hall, a narrow space lined with engraved skulls, Egyptian figurines, and a kaleidoscopic array of gemstones and crystals. In the back, the friends perused the menu, which consisted of cocktails inspired by different aspects of natural history. The most adventurous of the group ordered the Insectarium, an earthy honey-gin Negroni with a cricket-infused tincture, accompanied by a small piece of ant-ridden chocolate. The queasiest, looking away, opted for the Crystal Pass, a velvety Old-Fashioned incorporating oaky Scotch, bourbon, and mole sauce. The third friend, between sips of his Birds of the World (a tangy tequila-based concoction of elderflower, sunflower seeds, guava, and pineapple), began eavesdropping on a couple nearby, whose discussion had turned to mammalian politics. “Hyenas get a bad rep from ‘The Lion King,’ ” a man said to his date, “but they’re just kind of taking care of the leftovers, you know?” The eavesdropper, busy finishing a delectable pepper-chicken skewer, couldn’t agree more. Eventually, the place emptied out, and the trio took their leave to the hazy groove of a Khruangbin track. After all, the sun had set, the T. rex was still glowering, and one can never be too careful in a museum at night.

  • “Like a hug in a dish”

Brian Seibert has been contributing to The New Yorker since 2002. He is the author of “What the Eye Hears: A History of Tap Dancing,” which won an Anisfield-Wolf Book Award. His writing appears in the New York Times and the New York Review of Books. A Guggenheim fellow, he teaches at Yale University.

Dan Stahl is a member of The New Yorker’s editorial staff.

Rhoda Feng, who received the 2025 Nona Balakian Citation for Excellence in Reviewing, has also written about theatre and books for Artforum, the Boston Globe, and the Times Literary Supplement, among other publications.

Sheldon Pearce is a music writer for The New Yorker’s Goings On newsletter.

Taran Dugal is a member of The New Yorker’s editorial staff.

title: Company of Heroes 3's Operation Torch DLC ships off to North Africa in November, for new missions based around the Allied landings
author: Mark Warren
content:
Patton of attack

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. "If Relic can iron out some of those lingering campaign niggles, this could easily be an all-timer for WWII strategy buffs."

More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.

title: Days Gone studio's next PlayStation exclusive to be revealed and released in 2027, and it's not a sequel to the 2019 zombie-based action game, according to new report
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Deacon of hope.

Sony's Bend Studio, perhaps one of its lesser discussed development houses, has apparently been deep in development on its next title. The game is reportedly set to be announced in 2027, and released in the same year.

That's according to MP1st, citing "people aware of what's happening at Bend". Like Days Gone, Bend's next game is in third-person. The title is said to include co-op support, but no live service elements.

The report doesn't say whether the game is based on a new IP or an existing one, but it does state that it's not a sequel to Days Gone. The game is apparently "much further along in development" than we realise, which isn't entirely surprising considering Bend has been quiet for years.

The seven years since the release of Days Gone in 2019 have been tumultuous for Bend Studio. The developer revealed in 2022 its next project is a new IP that "builds upon the open-world systems of Days Gone" and includes multiplayer elements.

Two years later, a job post described a game in development at Bend as a triple-A live service project. That unannounced game was then cancelled in 2025, triggering a wave of layoffs at the studio that took place a few months later. Bend hasn't said a word since then.

It's now clear the studio hopped on its next project following the cancellation of that live service game. Seeing as 2026 is nearly over, we're not likely to be waiting much longer to see that mysterious game unveiled.

title: National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
In the summer of 1972, President Nixon’s reelection campaign financed the break-in at the Watergate complex with over $500,000 of campaign funds.1 Still, corrupt donors continued to fill the campaign’s coffers, allegedly using the Republican National Committee as a pass-through to avoid public scrutiny.2 After the Watergate hearings, Congress amended the Federal Election Campaign Act3 (FECA) in 1974, creating an enforcement agency, the FEC, and capping what campaigns, parties, and individuals could spend on or contribute to election-related activities.4 In a 2001 case known as Colorado II,5 the Supreme Court upheld FECA’s cap on a political party’s coordinated campaign expenditures.6 Coordinated expenditures — money spent “in cooperation, consultation or concert with, or at the request or suggestion of, a candidate”7 — were treated functionally as “contributions” because they offset a campaign’s expenses just like gifts of cash.8 Applying “closely drawn” scrutiny,9 Colorado II held that political-party coordinated-expenditure limits were sufficiently tailored to the important government interest of “combating political corruption.”10

Last Term, in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC11 (NRSC), a group of plaintiffs including Vice President J.D. Vance again challenged the constitutionality of political-party coordinated-expenditure restrictions under the First Amendment.12 This time, the petitioners had the Court’s jurisprudential trajectory, if not its precedent, on their side. The Roberts Court has slowly but inexorably rolled back FECA’s remaining campaign finance limitations.13 NRSC marked the next chapter in this project, freeing political parties to spend unlimited amounts in coordination with campaigns.14 Perhaps more foundationally, however, NRSC effected an unstated but avulsive change in the Court’s campaign finance jurisprudence by collapsing the doctrinal treatment of contributions and expenditures, thereby extending speech-like protection to all money in politics. This categorical treatment of money mischaracterizes the theoretical relationship between speech and money and protects a party’s bill-paying as equivalent to speech.

Four days before the 2022 midterm election, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), then–Senate candidate Vance, and then-Representative Steve Chabot sued the FEC and its commissioners, seeking to enjoin them from enforcing FECA’s coordinated-expenditure limits.15 Pursuant to section 310 of FECA, the plaintiffs moved to certify a question of the statute’s constitutionality to the en banc Sixth Circuit.16 Judge Cole of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio ruled that the plaintiffs had standing and raised a nonfrivolous issue, even if “Colorado II squarely applie[d].”17 Judge Cole certified the constitutional question as proposed by the plaintiffs and declined to certify “legislative facts” that he deemed more appropriate for judicial notice.18

The Sixth Circuit, self-aware of its role as a “warm-up for eventual Supreme Court review,”19 answered the certified question in favor of the FEC.20 Chief Judge Sutton,21 writing for the en banc court, held that Colorado II controlled.22 His opinion acknowledged that campaign finance doctrine had shifted since Colorado II but concluded that “it remains the Court’s job, not ours, to overrule it.”23 Some of the Chief Judge’s colleagues went a step further. Judge Thapar, writing a concurrence in name only, reasoned that First Amendment jurisprudence should follow New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen’s24 two-step history and tradition analysis.25 Judge Bush, answering the history-and-tradition call, concurred separately, contending that the history showed “no exception relevantly similar to the restriction at issue here.”26 Judge Readler dissented, claiming that the Sixth Circuit should not have been bound by a “largely obsolete precedent.”27 Judge Stranch, responding to her colleagues’ assorted attacks on Colorado II, concurred in the judgment and fervently defended the constitutionality of FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limits.28 With pointed brevity, Judge Bloomekatz wrote a two-sentence concurrence in the judgment noting that Colorado II remains binding precedent.29 As the Sixth Circuit predicted, the Supreme Court granted certiorari.30

Writing for the Court’s six conservative Justices, Justice Kavanaugh31 began by quoting Buckley v. Valeo,32 the Court’s foundational campaign finance opinion from 1976.33 A brief excursus on Buckley sets the stage for Justice Kavanaugh’s opinion: Buckley, which struck down FECA’s limits on independent expenditures, held that campaign expenditures and contributions implicated different First Amendment interests and that restrictions thereon were subject to different tiers of scrutiny.34 “[B]ecause virtually every means of communicating ideas in today’s mass society requires the expenditure of money,”35 the Buckley Court treated campaign expenditures as pure speech and thus subjected expenditure restrictions to “exacting scrutiny.”36 By contrast, contributions were primarily valuable for their expressive and associative content, not any speech inherent in gifts of money.37 Thus, the Court applied a less rigorous “closely drawn” scrutiny to FECA’s contribution restrictions and upheld them, regardless of whether the contribution was money or coordinated spending.38

In NRSC, Justice Kavanaugh ignored Colorado II’s functional characterization of coordinated expenditures as contributions. “[S]pending limits,” he wrote in the opinion’s opening paragraph, “necessarily abridge political parties’ freedom of speech.”39 Indeed, Justice Kavanaugh never referenced Colorado II’s central premise, that FECA treats coordinated expenditures as contributions.40 Instead, Justice Kavanaugh characterized the regulated transactions from the party’s perspective as spender rather than from the campaign’s perspective as recipient.41 Classified as a limit on spending rather than on contributions, FECA’s cap on coordinated party expenditures seems to burden the pure speech that Buckley protected.

Nevertheless — and without explaining the discrepancy — Justice Kavanaugh applied “closely drawn” scrutiny, the test that Buckley and Colorado II described as appropriate for limits on contributions.42 Recent Court precedent, he noted, had raised the threshold for what kind of tailoring counts as “closely drawn.”43 Thus, Justice Kavanaugh said, “we need not dwell on any subtle differences between the two tests.”44 Although the difference between “strict” and “closely drawn” scrutiny was decisive in Buckley, Justice Kavanaugh posited that “the question of which test to apply here is ultimately academic,” as both tests assess the government’s asserted interest in limiting speech and the fit between the interest and those limits.45

Justice Kavanaugh then rejected three hypothetical government interests for restricting campaign finance before turning to the only interest asserted by the Court-appointed amicus: preventing quid pro quo corruption or the appearance thereof.46 The theory of political-party coordinated-expenditure corruption posits that a corrupt donor would circumvent their individual contribution limits by donating to the party in the expectation, or on the explicit promise, that the money would be passed on to the campaign.47 Preventing corrupt actors from circumventing the base contribution limits is sufficiently important to justify burdening First Amendment speech, but a permissible restriction must be “closely drawn,”48 “narrowly tailored,”49 and “necessary for the interest it seeks to protect.”50

Where Colorado II applied only deferential review to the question of fit, later cases like McCutcheon v. FEC51 and FEC v. Ted Cruz for Senate52 sharpened the Court’s assessment of campaign finance tailoring.53 Thus, Justice Kavanaugh concluded that two less restrictive alternatives — earmarking and disclosure laws — made FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure restrictions unnecessary.54 Earmarking laws already make it illegal to circumvent base limits with contributions “directed through an intermediary or conduit.”55 Furthermore, FECA’s disclosure requirements obligate political parties and candidates to publicly disclose both expenditures and contributions, including coordinated expenditures.56 That transparency, according to the Court, arms the public and FEC with enough information to enforce earmarking rules.57 In order to prevent quid pro quo corruption, an individual’s base contribution limits are, according to Justice Kavanaugh, a first layer of prophylaxis; earmarking and disclosure requirements are a second and third layer; as a fourth layer of prophylaxis, FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limits were deemed “disproportionate”58 and not “necessary.”59

Nor would stare decisis save FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limits. Justice Kavanaugh considered “the egregiousness of the precedent’s error, the jurisprudential and real-world effects of the decision, and any cognizable reliance interests,”60 and concluded that all three factors militated in favor of overturning Colorado II.61 To demonstrate the egregiousness of Colorado II’s error, Justice Kavanaugh pointed to Justice Thomas’s “persuasive” 2001 dissent.62 As for real-world effects, Justice Kavanaugh noted that political parties have been relegated to “second-tier status” relative to outside groups like super PACs.63 Overruling Colorado II, he reasoned, would level the field.64 Finally, Justice Kavanaugh discounted any reliance that outside groups have in their relative advantage over parties without considering the differential effect such a ruling would have between national parties.65

Justice Kagan dissented.66 She did not dispute Justice Kavanaugh’s characterization of the political-party coordinated-expenditure limit as burdening pure speech or his description of the appropriate level of scrutiny. Instead, she addressed the granularities of campaign finance, showing how a motivated donor could use parties and their joint fundraising committees to circumvent the base contribution limit.67 Joint fundraising committees represent a candidate’s campaign, the relevant national party, and each of the fifty state parties, allowing a donor to combine each of his maximum donations into a single check ($7,000 to the campaign, $44,300 to the national party, and $10,000 to each of the state parties, totaling $551,300).68 As Justice Kagan articulated, donations to a hypothetical joint committee, the “John Smith Victory Fund,” require no earmarking to communicate a preferred candidate.69 The joint committee then disburses the contribution maximums to the national and state parties, which, within a few days, transfer that money back to the national party.70 Under Colorado II, the national party was limited in how much it could spend in coordination with John Smith’s campaign.71 Now, all $551,300 is potentially available to pay any of a campaign’s bills — from media spending to plumbing — completing the donor’s circumvention of the $7,000 base contribution limit.72 In Justice Kagan’s view, then, FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limitations appropriately prevented circumvention of the base limit and should have passed the fit test “with flying colors.”73

With the Roberts Court’s long process of campaign finance deregulation nearly at a close, it is worth reflecting on the unstated doctrinal evolution effectuated since Buckley: the collapse of any practical distinction between contributions and expenditures. In NRSC, Justice Kavanaugh confused the descriptive boundary between the two and further sharpened “closely drawn” scrutiny so that it approaches strict scrutiny. First, a contribution can be formalistically redescribed from the perspective of the donor, making it appear like an expenditure. And second, even if the Court chooses to apply “closely drawn” scrutiny, it will find any less restrictive means dispositive of a statute’s constitutionality. Although Justice Kavanaugh insisted that his opinion “does not address the statutory limits on coordinated expenditures by outside groups,” little in his logic is specific to political parties.74 Through this descriptive and doctrinal two-step, Justice Kavanaugh effectively erased any practical distinction between contributions and expenditures, thereby paving the way for all money in politics to receive categorical protection as pure speech. But money cannot be constitutionally protected speech in all circumstances. Money’s symbolic nature forecloses such a categorical treatment.

From a doctrinal perspective, the outcome in NRSC is not all that surprising. Since its inception, the contribution-expenditure dichotomy has been criticized for imperfectly answering whether a particular transaction amounts to speech.75 Most notably, several Justices have levied categorical criticisms, suggesting that money either always or never amounts to constitutionally protected speech.76 Indeed, Justice Thomas has long called for Buckley’s distinction between contributions and expenditures to be overruled.77 Over the last decade, the Court has repeatedly struck down FECA provisions that restricted contributions or their functional equivalents like coordinated expenditures.78 Along the way, the Court has gradually redescribed Buckley’s “closely drawn” scrutiny such that it now nearly resembles strict scrutiny. In Colorado II, the Court said that “closely drawn” scrutiny does not require overturning contribution limits for “unskillful tailoring.”79 In McCutcheon, however, the Court called the standard “lesser but still ‘rigorous’” relative to strict scrutiny.80 And in NRSC, Justice Kavanaugh further modified that description, labeling the Court’s review only “nominally ‘lesser but still rigorous.’”81 If, as Justice Kavanaugh wrote, the difference between strict and “closely drawn” scrutiny is “subtle” and ultimately “academic,” then both contributions and expenditures are, for practical purposes, protected like pure speech under the First Amendment.82 By treating contributions and expenditures with the same level of review, the Court has accomplished Justice Thomas’s goal in effect if not in name and extended the full protection of the First Amendment to all money in politics.

But money, standing alone, is not communicative; rather, it adopts symbolic meaning from a transaction and its context.83 To give more analytical content to the relationship between money and speech, we can identify two communicative components in every use of money. First, assuming no coercion, the fact of transaction makes an expression of value.84 That is, every free use of money contains the implied statement from each participant, “this is worth it to me.” That expression of value is present in every transaction and so, assuming that not every transaction is constitutionally protected speech, it cannot be sufficient to make a particular transaction constitutionally protected speech. The second communicative component of money relates to the underlying substance of a transaction. Money, in this way, symbolically adopts some meaning from the exchanged good. Whereas the expression of value is scalar, suggesting how much something is worth, the substantive component is directional, communicating, with enough context, the dimensions along which something has worth. Buying a sandwich, for instance, communicates something — perhaps a buyer’s hunger, her ethical commitment to veganism, or her generosity in feeding her companion — but its substantive meaning relies on more than the underlying good.85 That is, money becomes speech only through its context, not just its existence.

In NRSC, however, Justice Kavanaugh did not endeavor to assess what meaning, if any, was actually communicated by the regulated transactions.86 Instead, he treated money categorically, eschewing any attempt to determine whether the regulated transactions communicated something beyond the universal expression of value, “this is worth it to me.” Indeed, approximately three percent of the committees’ coordinated spending was, facially, not related to underlying political speech.87 The substantive component of those transactions — perhaps communicating a need for electricity or more campaign staffers — was decidedly not sacred political speech. But the other ninety-seven percent of transactions, “relate[d] to the ‘political advertising’” of Republican campaigns,88 was more difficult to assess. What, if anything, does it communicate for the NRSC to fund the speech of the campaigns it supports? Consider, for example, an email exchange regarding a coordinated expenditure between then–Senate candidate Vance’s campaign and the NRSC.89 After working with a media agency to plan, film, and edit a television commercial, Vance’s campaign forwarded the invoice to the NRSC for payment.90 The NRSC simply responded, “Received. Will process.”91 Does paying the campaign’s bill convert the advertisement into the NRSC’s own speech? This comment does not purport to offer an answer to such a difficult question. Perhaps symbolic speech doctrine could provide a more careful and accurate measure of when money symbolically adopts any underlying speech.92

But the Court has given up on this difficult, functional task. One could imagine an as-applied version of NRSC that threads this needle.93 To the extent that the NRSC was actually expressing its own speech, perhaps the coordination restrictions are poorly fitted to the government’s interest in preventing corruption. Justices Kavanaugh and Kagan would, presumably, still disagree on this “legally quite narrow” question.94 But whether the NRSC was speaking in the first place is knowable only by analyzing the communicative components of the transaction in question. Instead, the Court categorically links payment to speech, giving undue protection to bill-paying as speech.

The conclusion that money is speech has been criticized before,95 but NRSC thrusts it back into the spotlight by collapsing the doctrinal treatment of campaign expenditures and contributions. Thus, money receives categorical, speech-like constitutional protection, regardless of its use. Although the Court did not say as much in NRSC, the outcome is inevitable under Justice Kavanaugh’s logic. Indeed, at oral argument, Justice Kavanaugh seemed interested in discussing what little remains of FECA’s campaign finance restrictions.96 But such a categorical treatment of money is incongruous with the symbolic nature of money itself, which draws its speech-like meaning from the underlying substance of a given transaction. In NRSC, the Court rejected any factual analysis of the regulated transactions, categorically treating money in politics as speech. It did so without a theory of money’s relation to speech and erroneously concluded that a political party always speaks when it pays for its campaigns.

title: "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"
content:
I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

It's his immaturity….

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

title: As the controversy around AI-created video game copies continues, Anthropic seemingly restricts Claude's cloning abilities
author: Connor Makar
content:
DarioWare.

An update to Anthropic's Claude AI software has seemingly blocked the creation of outright clones or copies of existing games. Instead, Claude has been altered to only create "original" games.

Among the first to share news of the change was X user Chasm, who posted a screenshot showing the new rule, purportedly added around 27th October. "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets," it reads. "Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”.

While Anthropic is yet to issue an official statement on the new rule, technical staff member Addy Osmani commented beneath Chasm's post, confirming the change's legitimacy. He noted it was included because "using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy", but added that creating original games and those built with a user's own assets should still be possible.

Following the new rule's inclusion, users on GitHub shared newfound barriers they'd run into as a result. Reports included being blocked from creating digital modules for board games, and from recreating a commercially produced board game for personal use. Eurogamer has contacted Anthropic for comment on the rule change and its stance on AI game copies.

The modifications to Claude have appeared at a time when AI copies of games have drawn increasing ire, with game communities pushing back against them and developers pulling public-facing demos in fear of having their work stolen. AI-assisted copies of triple-A games have also emerged, including a version of Mario Kart 8 playable in an internet browser. However, this was taken down in a matter of days, presumably thanks to a legal notice from Nintendo.

Of course, even if Claude is prevented from making game copies, other AI tools, such as Deepseek, still lack similar restrictions. Until such measures are ubiquitous, the issue will continue. Given Claude's position as one of the most popular commercial AI tools out there, however, this will certainly make a dent in the problem.

title: Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature
author: James Archer
content:
Have you played...?

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

title: Acer Predator Atlas 8 (G3 Extreme) review
author: @pcgamer
content:
The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.

For

  • Excellent chip
  • Solid pricing for the specs

Against

  • Low storage in America
  • Mushy D-pad
  • Some software hiccups

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Intel's G3 Extreme is a mighty impressive chip, and easily the headline feature of Acer's Predator Atlas 8. If you're looking to get the best handheld Panther Lake chip right now, Acer has swooped in at pretty much the cheapest price point on the market.

And if that's all you want, the Atlas 8 has my blessing. It's a solid device that makes use of the chip and offers compromises in memory and storage capacity (in the American market) to bring that cost down. Not only that, but if you buy one right now, you get a heaping of goodies with it.

But if you don't need top-of-the-line specs to have a good time, the Atlas 8 instead becomes just one of many very, very solid, yet very, very expensive handhelds on offer in a time that has become worse and worse thanks to the memory crisis.

Buy if…

✅ You want the G3 Extreme but cheaper: The Atlas 8 undercuts both MSI and OneXPlayer in pricing for a G3 Extreme handheld.

Don't buy if…

❌ You play fighters or platformers primarily: The D-pad is mushy and lacks distinction, making it unsatisfying and a tad unruly.

The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.

The memory capacity is around average (Though lower than the high-end G3 Extreme offerings from MSI and OneXPlayer), and the storage is below average for a high-end handheld if you buy it in America.

Though 512 GB of storage isn't awful in a device you only want for gaming, the G3 Extreme is strong enough to take on even beefy, big-budget games, so it's a shame that the Atlas 8 can't hold all that many at once.

You are getting a strong feature set even outside of that chip, though. For one, TMR Sticks make for not only more efficient battery usage, but snappy, responsive controls. And you get Hall effect triggers too.

Ergonomics

At 860 grams, the Atlas 8 is a bit on the heavy side. It's balanced well, not feeling particularly heavy on either side, but you do notice that weight after long gaming sessions. I'm fond of the textured grips, but I do feel spoiled by the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 I used prior, thanks to its great feel and small cutaway between the screen and the grips.

However, I would simply pick a different handheld if you are planning on playing a heavy amount of fighting games or platformers, as the D-Pad is mushy, making it not only lacking in accuracy but generally unsatisfying to use. It's hard to make out when you actually hit buttons on the D-Pad, and it has very little distinction between different directions, making corner hits quite awkward. In Animal Well, I swapped to the thumbstick and never looked back.

Image 1 of 4

The triggers and bumpers are solid, though, and the macro buttons on the back are satisfying to hit. You can even use a toggle just under the triggers to swap them from micro switches to full travel. That's an on-the-fly level of customisation that's admirable at best, and unnoticeable at worst.

Everything else about the Acer Predator Atlas 8 feels high quality in terms of feel. It's sturdy, with buttons placed well, and they're satisfyingly clacky without being too loud. The sound on the triggers is too hollow for my liking, but they feel smooth to the touch and are plenty responsive.

Sound

Speaking of loud, the speakers built into the Atlas 8 can really thump. They are in the bottom left and bottom right of the device, near the screen, making them quite immersive in use. They're not the highest quality, with the clashing of steel sounding more tinny than I'd usually ask for, but they're certainly not bad given their size.

With fans set to auto and performance mode at the 35 W Turbo mode, the fans are noticeable (once again, I have been spoiled by the X20), especially in intensive games like Phantom Blade Zero. But they're not so loud that they would put me off using this handheld in its high-wattage mode. I measured the fans to be around 40 decibels at their peak (around a whisper), with it averaging 28-35 decibels in intensive games. Whilst benchmarking, that went up to the 50-decibel mark, though only very briefly.

Thermals

Acer says it has equipped the Atlas 8 with a custom Predator AeroBlade cooling, and in practice, it's certainly cooler than the likes of the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X and Lenovo Legion G S (though it doesn't beat the X20).

It certainly gets fairly hot internally, but with the fans pointing upwards, I never noticed any of that heat on my fingertips.

Software

Windows on a handheld can still be awkward. The Atlas 8 comes built in with Xbox's handheld software, which is somewhat like Microsoft's attempt at Steam, but it's not totally smooth sailing in any direction (though it's more efficient than Windows). For instance, you can't get Intel drivers through the Acer Predator software built into the device as you might expect, so you still have to go through the Intel updater or search the internet, except with a touchscreen. And the Xbox mode still opens up Steam independently if you want to play a Steam game.

Image 1 of 2

As well as this, the Atlas 8 has two dedicated buttons to open up Acer's software, the Acer Predator Sense, but it doesn't always work on the first try, and I haven't figured out exactly why this is yet. The button on the left-hand side opens up a quick bar-style version of the app to swap between performance modes, change resolution, etc. The button on the right-hand side opens the full-fat Predator Sense app, where you can get more granular with your customisation.

Though it's effectively the same setup as the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X, it's slower and more cumbersome. That seems to be the prevailing truth of pretty much any Windows-based handheld right now.

Battery life

I notice next to no difference between the 25W Quiet Mode and 30W Balanced Mode, with mere minutes being between them in the PC Mark 10 battery life gaming test.

However, Panther Lake's battery-saving mode (thanks to what Intel calls Endurance Gaming) is truly great, providing just under three hours of battery life. For less intensive use cases, I could see much better battery life. This Endurance mode can be flicked between three different modes, with one end bringing down power for better battery life, and the other bringing that power up in exchange for less battery life. The middle Balanced Mode is how I would use the handheld day-to-day.

The only downside here is that the very lightest mode on the Atlas 8 is currently 25 W, which is the max on Z2 Extreme handhelds. You can push that down below 25 W, but you have to set a custom wattage, which I'd wager many handheld owners don't want to mess with. For most, you will be using this between 25 W and 35 W day-to-day.

Aesthetics

Other than its fairly pretty face buttons, the Atlas 8 is a rather plain all-black gaming handheld. It goes without much intricate detailing (other than the Acer Predator RGB logo on the back and RGB rings around the thumbsticks).

As far as the display is concerned, you aren't getting any sort of fancy OLED here, but you do get a genuinely quite bright (500 nits) 16:10 WUXGA IPS display with Corning Gorilla Glass, making it decent in high-light environments. Importantly, I managed to play this out and about, and in front of a window, and could actually make out the game on screen, which is solid.

Value

As of right now, it seems like the only model of the Atlas 8 with a G3 Extreme chip that sells in America comes with 512 GB of storage. That means you are getting half the storage and 75% of the memory of the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ CG3EM for 72% of the cost. But, as far as performance is concerned, I got pretty much identical stats, even beating out the Claw in 3DMark and losing in storage performance. That extra 8 GB of memory is unlikely to provide a major uplift in games, though the extra storage will certainly come in handy. My money would be on the Atlas 8 here.

Then, for the same price, one could pick up the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (or the X for $300 less). Asus has the edge in ergonomics, look, thermals, screen, and storage capacity, but the G3 Extreme is a beast of a chip, handily handing Asus its butt in games. If you have got to pay upwards of $1,000 on a handheld right now, there's actually a good argument to be made for all three devices, though the Atlas 8 offers the best performance-to-price ratio.

It's a shame that Acer has to make little compromises to get that price down, but for $1,300, you will not get a better-performing gaming handheld in my book, and that's still quite impressive.

Acer Predator Atlas 8

The fact this is the cheapest way of getting Intel's G3 is both a boon for Acer and an indictment of the memory crisis. If you've gotta buy soon, this offers perhaps the best price-to-performance ratio above $1,000.
